problem: Navigation research mostly relies either on static recorded datasets (e.g., KITTI, PoseNet trajectories), which cannot support interactive decision-making or RL, or on synthetic or indoor simulators, which lack real-world visual diversity and city-scale extent. No public, interactive, photographic, city-scale environment existed for learning end-to-end goal-driven navigation.
motivation: The authors see navigation as an interactive learning problem, where perception, memory, planning and action should be learned together. Google Street View offers geolocated 360° panoramas and a real street connectivity graph with broad coverage, so it can be turned into a partially observed, first-person RL environment spanning whole cities. They release the environment, a privacy-vetted dataset (Manhattan and Pittsburgh), code and baseline agents so that long-range navigation such as the 'courier' task can be benchmarked.
key_idea: Turn Google Street View panoramas and their connectivity graph (~56K Manhattan + ~58K Pittsburgh nodes) into a Gym-style interactive RL environment. The agent sees cropped first-person views and must reach goals given as absolute lat/long coordinates (courier task). The paper releases this with instruction-following games and CityNav/MultiCityNav RL baselines.
insight: The results are reward-based, not SR/SPL. They show three things. (1) Splitting the agent into general pathways (conv encoder + policy LSTM) and a locale-specific goal LSTM supports multi-region training with only a small drop (e.g., Union Square 721 single vs 681 joint). It also supports transfer to a new region by training only a new goal LSTM (Wall Street 541 vs 782 single, oracle 809). (2) Performance on held-out goal areas degrades as the held-out squares grow: 724 on medium grid vs 605 on coarse grid, with fails rising from 0% to 2% (Table 3). (3) Absolute (lat, long) goal descriptors slightly outperform landmark-based descriptors on Union Square (721 vs 700, Table 4). The complete failure on South Shore (reward 1) is attributed to the curriculum, which uses Euclidean goal distance. That mismatches road distance in hilly terrain with rivers, so the curriculum design matters as much as the architecture.
method: StreetLearn dataset: Street View panoramas stored as protocol buffers, each with an equirectangular JPEG plus lat/long/altitude, pitch/roll/yaw, date and neighbour list. Covers Manhattan south of 81st St (~56K panos, 31.6 km²) and Pittsburgh (~58K panos). Faces and license plates are blurred and takedown requests are propagated to users.

Region definition by BFS: six connected sub-graphs (Wall Street, Union Square, Hudson River, CMU, Allegheny, South Shore; 7K–18K nodes each) are grown by breadth-first search from a central panorama to a fixed graph depth, for training and transfer.

Environment interface: C++ engine projects equirectangular panoramas to first-person views, wrapped by a Python OpenAI-Gym-style API. The observation is a 60° crop resized to 84×84 RGB. Actions rotate yaw/pitch, zoom, or move forward to a neighbour within a 30° bearing tolerance. RL agents use 5 discrete actions: forward, ±22.5°, ±67.5°. Optional observations include the graph image, yaw bins, neighbour traversability, ground-truth direction (for imitation learning) and instruction thumbnails.

Games: coin_game; courier_game, where the goal is a lat/long pair reached within 100 m, reward is proportional to shortest-path length, early shaping reward applies within 200 m, and episodes last 1000 steps; curriculum_courier_game, which grows the goal range from 500 m to the full graph; and instruction games (goal / incremental / step_by_step) with natural-language instructions plus thumbnails.

CityNav agent: conv encoder, then a goal LSTM that receives the goal descriptor, visual features, previous action and reward, and has an auxiliary heading prediction; then a policy LSTM outputting policy and value. Trained with IMPALA (256 actors, batch 256, unroll length 50); comparable results reported with 16 actors on one GPU desktop.

MultiCityNav agent: shared conv encoder and policy LSTM with one goal-LSTM pathway per region (512 actors). For transfer to a new region only a new goal LSTM is trained; the encoder and policy LSTM are frozen.
Oracle: BFS shortest path on the panorama graph gives the next panorama and bearing, providing an upper bound on courier rewards.

setting.backbone: CityNav / MultiCityNav: CNN encoder (as in Mnih et al. 2016) + goal LSTM + policy LSTM, trained from scratch with deep RL (IMPALA actor-critic)
setting.training_data: Online RL interaction in StreetLearn Street View regions (Manhattan / Pittsburgh), with a goal-distance curriculum and reward shaping. The generalisation experiments train for 1B steps; no external data.
setting.observation: monocular first-person RGB (60° crop of Street View panorama, 84×84) + absolute goal lat/long + previous action and reward
setting.action_space: 5 discrete actions: move forward to the neighbouring panorama on the street graph (no-op if no edge in view), rotate ±22.5°, rotate ±67.5°
setting.simulator: StreetLearn (Google Street View panoramas + connectivity graph)
setting.privileged: none (goal given as absolute lat/long coordinates; agent never sees the graph or its own position; heading prediction is only an auxiliary training loss)

numbers_note: Environment/dataset paper; the only benchmark is the new StreetLearn courier task, measured by average goal reward per 1000-step episode (not SR/SPL). Regions are treated as separate 'other:' benchmarks. There is no official train/test split: courier results are measured in the training region, so the split is labelled 'test'. Table 3 does not state which region was used. The instruction-following games are described but no results are reported for them. CityNav/MultiCityNav are the authors' agents from Mirowski et al. 2018, reported here as baselines.
results: Single-region CityNav agents reach 85–97% of oracle returns in New York (e.g., Wall Street 782 vs oracle 809, Union Square 721 vs 750). They do worse in Pittsburgh (CMU 473 vs 755) and fail completely on South Shore (1 vs 737). A jointly trained MultiCityNav agent over 5 regions drops only slightly in NYC (e.g., Wall Street 745). Transfer to Wall Street by training only a new goal LSTM yields 541. Held-out goal areas give 724 (medium grid) and 605 (coarse grid) vs 719 on training goals, and (lat, long) goals beat landmark goals on Union Square (721 vs 700).
limitations: Static environment: no dynamic elements, discrete panorama-jumping actions, and a fixed street topology that cannot be altered or regenerated; coverage is limited to Manhattan and Pittsburgh.

The RL baselines need large compute (256–512 IMPALA actors, very high memory for panorama caching). They fail on hilly regions such as South Shore because the curriculum uses Euclidean rather than road distance.
Instruction-following games are introduced without any reported baseline results; evaluation reuses the training regions rather than an official held-out split.
builds_on: CityNav / MultiCityNav (Learning to Navigate in Cities Without a Map, Mirowski et al. 2018)
